title: Willpower: Rediscovering the Greatest Human Strength
author: Roy F. Baumeister
John Tierney
target_audience: Adults seeking to improve self-control or self-discipline
Students of psychology, neuroscience, or behavioral science
Professionals interested in productivity and habit formation
General readers interested in human motivation and behavior change
core_themes: The scientific understanding of willpower and self-control
Willpower as a finite but renewable resource
Factors that strengthen or deplete willpower
Implications of willpower in everyday life, health, and achievement
primary_purpose: To explore the science behind willpower, reveal how self-control works, and provide evidence-based guidance for improving self-discipline and making better life choices.

structure_format.narrative_style: Accessible, engaging, and research-driven, blending scientific studies with real-life anecdotes
structure_format.organization: Organized into thematic chapters covering the nature of willpower, famous experiments, historical case studies, and practical advice
features: Clear breakdowns of scientific research and experiments
Practical applications and advice at the end of each chapter
Case studies and stories involving famous figures and ordinary people

key_concepts_lessons: Willpower operates like a muscle: it can be depleted through use but also strengthened with practice.
Ego depletion: exerting self-control in one domain can reduce willpower for subsequent tasks.
Blood glucose plays a role in willpower and self-regulation.
Setting clear goals, monitoring progress, and establishing routines are effective ways to conserve and build willpower.
Small acts of self-control can accumulate, improving overall discipline.
Understanding personal limitations and planning for willpower failures can prevent setbacks and promote resilience.
notable_features: Bridges experimental psychology, neuroscience, and everyday experience
Mixes rigorous scientific analysis with humor and relatable stories
cultural_historical_context: Published during a period of rising interest in self-help, behavioral economics, and the neuroscience of habits, the book popularized the idea that self-control could be understood and trained like a muscle—bridging academic research and mainstream conversation.
reception_impact: Bestseller status; acclaimed for accessible science writing and practical value
Helped popularize research on self-regulation and 'ego depletion'
Influenced the field of self-help and productivity literature
Some subsequent research has revisited or questioned specific elements of the ego depletion model, sparking ongoing academic debate
comparable_titles: The Power of Habit by Charles Duhigg
Self-Control: Its Kingship and Majesty by William George Jordan
Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman
